1.point: The chapter will show the traveller finishing the road back among people while still with God, as the friends of God in the Munajat and Imam Ali's words to Kumayl do.
steps: Put the Munajat line (secret with God, open work for Him) before the reader.
Show Imam Ali describing the same people to Kumayl: bodies here, spirits in the highest abode, calling people to God.
Recall Chapter Twelve's sober return in a sentence and say this chapter follows the traveller the rest of the way.

2.point: Annihilation closes only the first of four journeys; in the second God carries the traveller through His names and returns him to himself as a servant.
steps: Name the four journeys and their order.
Identify the first journey with the road the book has followed so far, ending in annihilation, a quarter of the way.
Explain that the remaining journeys are made 'by God', the traveller carried by His wilaya once the self is gone.
State what the second journey examines: what is reflected in the heart, God's names and attributes.
State where it ends: baqa', sobriety, the traveller a servant of God, still facing God.

3.point: The third journey returns the servant to creation, which he now sees as God's names at work, and the fourth keeps him among people, still with God, to guide them.
steps: Describe the third journey: back through the worlds to the material world, seeing them as manifestations of the names; outcome certainty (Ibrahim).
Show that this certainty is to be passed on: he can inform others.
Describe the fourth journey: among people, knowing how all returns to God, able to guide them.
Show why the fourth journey is needed for living among people: after the first journey alone it is very difficult; after the fourth it is easy because he sees God in people.

4.point: The full return is the Prophet's and the Imams'; others are called to travel towards it as far as God allows.
steps: State the Sheikh's limits: third journey for high-calibre mystics, fourth for the Prophet and Imams.
Give Tabataba'i's parallel judgment: holding both worlds is perhaps exclusive to prophets, awliya and whoever God wishes.
Show the Prophet holding both worlds (states beyond any archangel; 'I am only a man like you').
Separate office from station: prophethood is exclusive, the station of wilaya is not, and the Prophet's call implies the road is open.
Draw the consequence for the rest of us: follow him by staying in society while travelling.

5.point: Imam al-Husayn's life shows the whole return: before God among his household at Arafah, and with and for his people at Karbala.
steps: Take Khomeini's instruction to look at the Day of Arafah supplication as the example of a prophet-like life that also rose against wrongdoers.
Set the Arafah scene: the Imam among his household, before God as a beggar, asking for fear of God as if seeing Him.
Carry him to Karbala: he stayed with his people and stood for them.
Close the chapter: the completed journey returns the traveller to people while with God.

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: Opens with the Munajat line (secret with God, open work) and introduces Imam Ali's description of the same people to Kumayl; this is the hook and the image the chapter returns to.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Reads the Kumayl hadith back against the Munajat line (bodies here, spirits above, calling people to God) and names the four journeys as the frame the chapter will use.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: Recalls Chapter Twelve in one sentence and states what this chapter will establish: the traveller comes back among people and stays with God, as far as Karbala.

¶4.label: advance
¶4.why: Supplies the four journeys and their order, the step the whole section rests on.

¶5.label: advance
¶5.why: Identifies the first journey with the road travelled so far in the book and lands the 'one quarter of the way' claim.

¶6.label: advance
¶6.why: Explains what 'by God' means for the remaining journeys: the self gone, the traveller carried by God's wilaya.

¶7.label: advance
¶7.why: Turns the night-prayer line into the second journey's content: God's guardianship lived, and the traveller examining what is reflected in the heart. The 'harder and more delightful' remark is extra, but the paragraph supplies a needed step.

¶8.label: advance
¶8.why: States what the second journey takes him through, God's names and attributes, and sets the limit (only the Prophet has no one above him) that Section 4 uses.

¶9.label: advance
¶9.why: Supplies where the second journey ends: baqa', sobriety, 'a servant of Allah', and places Chapter Twelve's sober return on the map.

¶10.label: restate
¶10.why: Summarises ¶5 and ¶9. The only new note, that he still faces God rather than people, is the hinge to Section 3 and could open ¶11 instead.

¶11.label: advance
¶11.why: Describes the third journey: back through the worlds, all seen as manifestations of the names, with certainty as the outcome.

¶12.label: support
¶12.why: Explains malakut and ties the Ibrahim verse to the third journey's outcome, 'reassurance about everything'; ¶11 relies on the verse and ¶13 builds on the certainty.

¶13.label: advance
¶13.why: Adds the step that the certainty is passed on: he can inform others, becomes 'the knower', and Mutahhari gives the third journey the purpose of guiding people.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: Describes the fourth journey: among people, shown how everything returns to God, able to tell people harms and benefits.

¶15.label: advance
¶15.why: Raises the needed problem: a traveller who has finished only the first journey cannot easily live among people (the drunk travellers, Tabataba'i's gnostic of thirty years). ¶16 answers it.

¶16.label: advance
¶16.why: Resolves ¶15: after the fourth journey mixing with people is easy because he sees God in them; this is the 'among people, with God' half of the point.

¶17.label: aside
¶17.why: Returns to the Munajat line (secret with God, open among people) already laid down in ¶1 and ¶2 and introduces the Imam al-Sadiq story for a lesson in hidden zuhd. Nothing in ¶18 or later uses it; the callback belongs to the chapter's close rather than to this section's chain.

¶18.label: restate
¶18.why: Restates the section's point, which ¶13, ¶14 and ¶16 have already established.

¶19.label: advance
¶19.why: States the limits: third journey open to high-calibre mystics, fourth to the Prophet and Imams, and recalls the limit set in ¶8.

¶20.label: support
¶20.why: Shows what the fourth journey looks like in the Imams, inner knowledge given within the law, which supports ¶19's claim that the fourth journey belongs to them. The Chapter Six and Twelve callbacks are not used afterwards.

¶21.label: advance
¶21.why: Brings Tabataba'i's judgment: the rank is perhaps exclusive to prophets, awliya and whoever God wishes. The 'whoever God wishes' is what ¶23 and ¶25 build on.

¶22.label: support
¶22.why: Gives the Prophet as the instance of holding both worlds (states beyond any archangel; the verse); ¶23 reads this contrast directly.

¶23.label: advance
¶23.why: Separates office from station: prophethood exclusive, the station of wilaya not, and the Prophet's call implies the road is open. The first sentence repeats ¶22.

¶24.label: advance
¶24.why: Explains the al-Ahzab verse and draws the consequence for the reader: following him means staying in society from the start of the road.

¶25.label: restate
¶25.why: Summarises ¶19, ¶21 and ¶23; the conclusion has already been reached.

¶26.label: advance
¶26.why: Takes Khomeini's pointer to the Day of Arafah supplication as the example of a life that prayed and rose against wrongdoers, and declares what the section will do.

¶27.label: support
¶27.why: Supplies the Arafah scene from the Mafatih (among his household, facing the Ka'ba, hands raised like a beggar) and the request about his heart; ¶28 and ¶29 depend on it.

¶28.label: restate
¶28.why: Draws out what ¶27 already showed: among his household and before God as a beggar. The reading of the quotation (to fear God as if seeing Him) is a single clause; the rest repeats.

¶29.label: advance
¶29.why: Carries the Imam from Arafah to Karbala: with his people to the last and, on Khomeini's reading, for them. The Munajat line about wielding the sword closes the chapter's opening image.

¶30.label: restate
¶30.why: Restates the chapter thesis and the points of Sections 2, 3 and 4. The Ashura 'express sympathy' sentence is a new remark the argument does not use.

¶31.label: aside
¶31.why: A bridge to the next chapter that poses a question this chapter does not answer; cutting it loses nothing the argument uses.
